newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major faces parliamentary war of attrition.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major faces parliamentary war of attrition.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, fighting to hang on to power, faces an exhausting parliamentary war of attrition after the opposition tore up long-standing cooperation deals with the government in a row over cheating.
Ruling Conservative party managers were looking forward to parliament's Christmas break as a chance to rally supporters for the drive to the election, due in May at the latest.

But the opposition made clear on Wednesday they would not let up in their campaign to bring down the deeply divided government, which last week lost its majority after a Labour party by-election victory.

The opposition drew first blood on Tuesday night, when the government was ambushed in a vote on an amendment to a bill on stalking -- the practice of harassing victims by following them around -- and lost by 179 votes to 172.
"This government is devious. Cheating has become a way of life with this government," said Labour deputy leader John Prescott.
Major drew comfort from figures on Wednesday which showed unemployment last month fell to 1.93 million. It was the first time the total had dropped below two million for six years.
"They are not good they are magnificent," Major said of the unemployment figures.
When the Conservatives came to power in 1979, unemployment stood at 1.09 million before peaking at 2.98 million in 1992.

There was no immediate threat to the government's survival from Tuesday's vote but the result underlined Major's parliamentary problems after the collapse of the unwritten codes which govern cooperation between the opposing sides.
The row centres on "double counting" in a key vote on Monday on European fishing policy. Major won, ensuring his survival.

But the opposition said the government inflated its support by offering both Labour and Liberal Democrat party managers the same three names of MPs for "pairing" -- a system to allow MPs to be absent for key votes without affecting the overall result.
Conservative party managers denied the charges. But former Conservative parliamentary manager Archie Hamilton said: "I think it was something the government might now regret."

Behind the detailed argument about the arcane rules of parliamentary procedure, the row shows a new level of bitterness between the government and the opposition -- and a new level of desperation by a government which has lost its majority.
This parliamentary session has seen Major fail in attempt after attempt to rebuild his political fortunes.
It began in disarray in October when Major was forced to backtrack and agree to Labour calls for laws on stalking and sex offenders, giving voters the impression he was losing his grip.

Under pressure from rank and file MPs, the government then decided to ignore calls to outlaw all handguns, proposing instead a limited ban, infuriating relatives of children killed in the Dunblane school massacre earlier this year.
The budget failed to grab voters with its one point cut in income tax. Labour's poll lead continued to soar, touching 37 points in one survey and staying above 20 points in the rest.

Sleaze returned to haunt Major when a junior minister, David Willetts, was forced to resign over allegations he tried to influence a probe into whether another minister accepted cash to ask parliamentary questions.
Chronic splits over Europe surged into view time and again, battering Major's efforts to rebuild party unity.
